Our investigation centers on four distinct co-adding approaches applied to incoherent sources, and we derived corresponding point spread functions for each. It's found that only two rescaling algorithms result in co-added images with well-defined point spreads, and we further develop three well-defined psf-convolution operators for each of these algorithms to verify their correctness. These operators are not merely theoretical; they can be applied to actual co-adding processes to improve the uniformity of exposure times in the final co-added image, thereby minimizing systematic biases in scientific measurements such as the magnitudes of point sources and clustered sources with spatially variable point spreads. Our study's code is code and will be particularly useful in deep learning simulations requiring large training datasets of co-added images. This code is especially relevant for astronomical image analysis.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence.  They specifically considered the dyadic tree, where each node is paired with a Gaussian free field, generating an infinite-dimensional process with a branching structure.  They demonstrated that one instance of this process can be constructed from independent realizations of the Dyson model at multiple scales in noise realizations.  We extend this model by showing the stochastic nature of solutions to a rough version of the KPZ equation across a dyadic tree, relying on estimates of the Dyson model and avoiding any analytic continuation between equations.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm.

The verification process for quantum computation is crucial, particularly when dealing with untrusted quantum processors. Currently, the fastest known protocol for verifying classical output from quantum computation has a time complexity of O(n^3), relying on quantum RAM. Despite numerous developments in quantum computation verification protocols, cloud-based computing remains the fastest option. Our research introduces a novel, straightforward protocol with a time complexity of O(n^2) on quantum RAM, outperforming existing research and confirming that verification of classical output in quantum computation can be achieved more efficiently than through cloud computing.

Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically is crucial for training deep learning frameworks for biologically relevant tasks such as segmentation, shape analysis, and mechanical property estimation. For years, researchers have attempted to create fake cell shapes using voxel-based or polygon mesh representations, but these approaches have significant limitations due to their inability to represent complex geometry. We propose using level sets of signed distance functions to represent shapes, which allows for compact representation, easy manipulation, and diffusion, in contrast to both voxel-based and polygon mesh representations. This approach enables the creation of diverse, photorealistic cell shape datasets by adding shape diversity to real cell images, which can then be used for generating synthetic time-lapse videos for training data augmentation and time-lapse completion. Our method is open-source and available at https://cells.ahls.helsinki.fi/sdf.

Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning agents that can train without prior knowledge, our work demonstrates two successful methods for this type of off-policy model-free learning, and we provide a comparison evaluating their suitability for biologically realistic models. Specifically, we show how these agents develop internal maps, even when initiated from pre-defined navigational targets, and through this process, they discover key metrics including optimal policies, state values, and state-feature mappings, all essential for spatial cognition. Furthermore, we evaluate two methods of target creation, revealing that though both are valid, one leads to more efficient learning in terms of sample usage. This finding suggests that interactively adapting targets during interaction, rather than relying on pre-defined targets, might spatial cognition, enabling agents to successfully build internal maps and achieve their goals.

To evaluate the efficiency of event-chain Monte Carlo algorithms for complex simulations, specifically in two-dimensional models of hard-disk dipoles tethered together, researchers assess their performance through multiple试验s, measuring integration time-step effects and contrasting their outcomes with conventional local Metropolis simulations, then juxtaposing these results with theoretical expectations of pure diffusion to understand how long the system's dynamics genuinely persist beyond standard random behavior. Furthermore, different ECMC algorithm variants are explored, including their parameter optimizations, 30-, 100-, and 1000-molecule models at various densities, simulating a range from low to high density conditions to investigate how long individual trajectories truly last.

This research introduces a novel approach to solving the sound event localization and detection problem using convolutional recurrent neural networks, combined with multi-scale audio feature extraction techniques, for optimal classification and direction of sound sources.

In traditional communication systems, signal interference is generally viewed unfavorably as it suppresses individual user signals and complicates data recovery. Nonetheless, there are specific applications like network coding and physical layer network coding where mutual signal mixing serves as a vital component. To tackle wireless communication challenges, we leverage the positive aspect of in-order signal superposition—referred to as simultaneous transmission—starting from the channel mixing capability provided by MIMO channels. We initially examine single-frequency transmission and move on to examine multi-frequency transmission within MIMO systems. Notably, our analysis reveals that the number of successful messages in multi-frequency transmission scales linearly with the product of frequency numbers, and this relationship also applies to real-world systems implementing these techniques.

Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a fundamental part of the classical short time Fourier transform (STFT). We investigate the underlying mathematics of these spectrograms, focusing on the properties of their zero sets. Theory tells us that these zeros are complex to analyze due to their high complexity and interdependence. We simplify this by concentrating on less complex subsets of spectrogram zero sets. Our research involves the mathematical characterization of boundary cases in these simplified zero sets. Using this characterization, we are able to create explicit representations of unit modulus functions in Lp spaces, function spaces encoded by BMO, and Hahn Banach theorems. We also establish key inequalities relating to Riesz kernels, understanding the interplay between STFT spectrograms and Riesz kernels.

We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple coexisting stable limit cycles in systems of phase oscillators with random connections, and we extend this approach to identify multiple stable patterns in complex networks including small-world architectures and systems dynamics. This method leverages a reduced dimensionality approach and will be demonstrated through numerous examples that illustrate its efficacy and applicability.

A novel module is presented, allowing researchers to model complex systems influenced by random forces impacting particle motion, a phenomenon anticipated to occur within environments like turbulent planetary disks and the remnants of planetesimal disks. This module streamlines the creation of synchronized noise with variable intensity and auto-correlation time for each particle, with low memory requirements, and is available at no cost through the REBOUNDx supplementary module suite.

Key aspects of quantum science include precise measurement and feedback mechanisms, offering wide-ranging benefits from advanced quantum technology to the conversion of information into work within quantum thermodynamics. Mathematical explanations, mainly based on quantum stochastic calculus or operator-algebraic theory, effectively describe these processes, but their complexity limits their practical use for designing and understanding engineers' insights into quantum systems. This book focuses on presenting new methods for model-based quantum feedback control, grounded in concepts familiar from modern control theory, including state estimation, stochastic Lyapunov theory, linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) and linear quadratic quadratic (LQR) control, as well as advanced nonlinear model predictive control. These methodologies are applicable not only to Gaussian quantum systems, characterized by continuous measurement and state, but also to general nonlinear quantum systems undergoing state collapse during measurement, including innovative topics like information-to-work conversion and quantum control through finite-level feedback, all essential for future quantum technologies.

In a long and narrow container with a horizontal axis, two discs are contained within it, with at least one of them having a size comparable to the container's width. Various ways of arranging the discs are classified based on the position of each disc relative to the container's obstacles, with these arrangements being represented as configurations with specific numbers of left and right disc positions. A system was established to analyze these discs in different conditions, with the discs representing a mesoscopic scale that is larger than the container's width but smaller than its length. When the system was placed in a container much larger than the disc sizes and subjected to compression, distinct, self-similar arrangements emerged that did not change with the system's pressure. Various aspects of these discs, including their positions, velocities, sizes, and the space separating them, were analyzed in this study, with these factors influencing the resulting arrangement of the discs. By representing these arrangement of the discs in a two-dimensional space with specific axes, distinct, distinct regions were found corresponding to different configuration types. To understand these arrangement of the discs, a method of mapping these configuration to a liquid-gas system were found that did not depend on the number of discs, with these system exhibiting distinct, distinct characteristics that influenced by a parameter representing disc sizes, with parameters influencing these arrangement of the discs and exhibiting distinct, distinct transitions in behavior, with these arrangement of the discs and exhibiting distinct, distinct characteristics that do not influence by disc sizes.

Research into El Ni\~no's two primary forms - East Pacific and Central Pacific - has become a significant area of study within climate science, particularly with regard to their distinct impacts on global seasonal rainfall. Predicting which type of El Ni\~no will occur is crucial. Traditional climate models often fail to accurately simulate this phenomenon. However, Cliv^e Harper's research suggests that El Ni\~no's behavior can be understood through its decomposition into two fundamental modes - each corresponding to one of the prevailing strategies. One study, based on satellite data, analyzes global precipitation during 2000-2018 and quantifies their global rainfall contributions. It reveals that East Pacific-associated patterns consistently produce significant global rainfall deviations, whereas Central Pacific patterns have a predominantly local effect with opposing signs during positive and negative phases. Furthermore, their simultaneous occurrence can generate substantial global rainfall deviations. During periods when Central Pacific patterns are stronger than usual - as was the case in 2018 - their ability to significantly influence global rainfall becomes largely irrelevant. Moreover, East Pacific patterns are typically preceded by strong Central patterns, whereas simultaneous occurrence of both patterns can lead to significant global rainfall deviations. Notably, timeframes with strong Central patterns but weaker El Ni\~no occurrence - such as 2018 - have experienced record low global rainfall deviations. Conversely, instances of exceptionally strong El Ni\~no occurrence - as happened in 2015 and 2017

Evidence of massive black holes exists in many small galaxies, but their exact mass and formation process remains unclear. Evidence of a specific formation process may be found in certain characteristics of these objects, observed during a particular period of time predicted for certain galaxy evolution theories. We have identified a potential sign of this process in unusual behavior from a particular object called CO-55, located in a galaxy known as Centaurus A. Its movement patterns and other characteristics suggest the presence of a massive black hole with properties unusual for a typical massive black hole, possibly forming as predicted by a specific theory related to the development of galaxies.

In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological currents are amplified through correlation effects, though the link between this geometric feature and the material's quantum state remains unclear. Our study employs theoretical models, theoretical, and numerical tools to investigate the influence of geometric properties on the quantum states of a quasicrystalline flat-band system, specifically an iridium-based kagome quasicrystal, kagome Moore-Barker phase. Our results show that the geometric properties of the electron-electron interaction distinguishable from those of single-particle operators lead to many-body wave functions with distinct topological characteristics, indicating that topological currents are a product of both orbital geometry and interorbital interactions. Our research underscores the significance of interorbital interaction effects in flat-band systems. Our results indicate that quantum properties such as superconductivity, characterized by a zero-bias peak in the tunneling density of states, can be mapped to single-orbital Hamiltonians with effective vector potentials, providing potential pathways for detecting topological currents experimentally and yoking them to emergent quantum phenomena.

Understanding how genomic variation influences specific traits is key to unlocking various biological processes. Although large-scale projects like the Human Cell Map have generated vast databases of genome-wide chromatin maps, pinpointing the exact functional impact of genetic polymorphisms remains complex. In contrast, a new study takes advantage of existing data to identify which regions in the genome are more likely to be affected by certain inherited traits in humans. The analysis focuses on Ensembl variations associated with specific traits, checking if they overlap with chromatin maps from different cell types, including 127 different types from the Human Cell Map. The study reveals that SNPs related to specific traits are more likely to be in regions that match those traits-related characteristics, and also finds that SNPs related to certain metabolic disorders are more likely in areas with active enzyme sensitivity. Furthermore, the study discovers a potential link between SNPs and the disruption of topologically associating domains, and observes that SNPs associated with growth and metabolism are more likely in regions regulated by the activity of the CTCF protein.

This study identifies and classifies 2-designs that satisfy specific conditions and have specific automorphism properties. A non-trivial 2-design's automorphism group can either be an instance of the previously documented examples described in this research or a specific subgroup within a larger group of automorphisms that corresponds to a geometric linear transformation involving a prime number.

This study examines electronic correlation within confined hydrogen, helium and lithium ions in their base states using entropy measures. Different wavefunctions are used to better account for inter-electronic interactions. The resulting entropy values show sensitivity to these interactions. In situations of extremely tight confinement, Coulomb effects are minimized and models treating particles as independent or non-interacting pairs in an impenetrable sphere are increasingly applicable. Energy estimates derived from these models align well with existing literature values.

The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To analyze low acceleration gravity, we've compiled a database of binary stars consisting of components with spectral classes up to G8, covering distances from around 100 parsecs to 1000 parsecs, via spectroscopic observations. This star database consists of over 80 systems consisting of over 160 components, using radial velocity data collected over over a century. To determine their orbital characteristics, we used MCMC methods, resulting in the calculation of the ratio of observed to predicted separations when using Newton's law of universal gravitation. This observation suggests that long-term stable wide binary systems are predominantly consistent with the standard gravitational model. To test gravitational stability, we've used close binary star data, resulting in the identification of over 80 long-period binary systems, resulting in these being dynamically stable at a level of over 99%. To analyze gravitational effects, we've used simulated binary star data, resulting in these having simulated non-Newtonian properties. Comparing our observed binary star data to these simulated non-Newtonian properties suggests long-period wide binary systems consistent with Newton's law of universal gravitation. This suggests long-period binary systems with wide separations are difficult to distinguish from those governed by modified gravity theories.

To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate an ideal that encapsulates its logical meaning through polynomial equations. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory.

Financial time series may exhibit similar dynamic behaviors when analyzed locally, which can be analyzed using non-linear time series analysis. Specifically, this study utilizes cross-recurrence plot analysis to identify the leading time series driving a pair of synchronized time series. To automate and objective unit detection, wavelet transformation is applied to decompose time series into specific frequency bands. This method, often based on visual inspection or expert knowledge, is optimized through automated multi-scale cross-correlation analysis. This research presents a solution that combines these techniques to automatically detect significant units of time series where dynamic relationships are non-linear and depend on past time steps. A following step of time lag analysis will help understand these relationships on a global scale. A case study will demonstrate the proposed method on a gold and USD price dataset, comparing it to a linear approach based on delay coordinates.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for seconds after the initial pulse, making them enduring inertial effects.

Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on behavior IDs that are based on past user-ad interactions. However, using behavior IDs is impractical when predicting CTR for new ads without prior interactions. To overcome these limitations, our approach utilizes ad visuals to enhance the performance of CTR prediction models. We introduce multiple contributions: (a) for non-interactive ads, we employ virtual interactions to generate additional training data using deep generative models; (b) for deep learning-based CTR models, we propose a prediction error correction layer to accelerate fine-tuning during transfer learning; (c) for traditional CTR models, we suggest using deep learning models to pre-calibrate key features. We validated our technique through large-scale experiments using real industry data and consistently showed improved performance.

Traditionally, business process management concentrated on organized, task-based processes, but the rise in importance of intellectual processes necessitates a comprehensive approach that considers both organized and intellectual processes within organizations. The current methods for modeling process knowledge still fall short in addressing processes with semi-structured steps as significant as those with organized steps. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach incorporating organizational process model elements that represent semi-structured steps along with a corresponding method to map representation methods to those elements. Our framework, grounded in the APISMA method, enables the exploration of alignment between a organization's structural setup and its process knowledge, ensuring consistency in the process model. Furthermore, we develop criteria for comparing process models, enabling modelers to evaluate knowledge-intensive processes more effectively, while maintaining open compatibility between mapping methods.

Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from gas emission and reducing solar irradiation reaching the ground.
A stochastic model of photons and emitters formation and scattering is proposed,
which accounts for random photon attenuation by emitters and resulting fire
optical thickness. By generating random emitters in a defined volume, we simulate
photons and emitters formation in a fire column and calculate the irradiance at
ground level. By integrating the code with solar flux and solar panel efficiency,
we evaluate panels' energy production under fire conditions.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measurements. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual differences, and our findings indicate that comparing two groups has relatively minor effects, but can have a significant influence on detecting individual differences. In multisite studies, it is essential to account for site effects, as an omission can result in false positives, increased power, and reduced effect sizes, regardless of whether we are measuring individual variation or detecting group effects, based on our simulation results. Furthermore, based on a real-world analysis of brain networks from high-risk infants, we recommend that researchers adopt junction correction when investigating multisite effects and utilize models that compare site effects to highlight genuine individual disparities.

Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature.

Recent developments in NLP for code-mixed languages have facilitated the creation of language models, such as word embeddings. Nonetheless, most current word embeddings models depend on supervised training methods that demand extensive labeled training data, a resource that is often scarce in mixed code-speaking communities. This paper investigates the potential of training contextual word embeddings without supervision for code-mixed Turkish, an underresearched language. We evaluate the effectiveness of word2vec, a word-based embedding method, and contextual embedding methods including bi-LSTM, Skip-Thought, and multi-LSTM approaches. Our results show that these methods can produce functional embeddings even when trained on limited datasets containing noise and linguistic variations inherent to social media posts. Additionally, these embeddings outperform static embeddings in downstream tasks, such as social media post classification.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the isotope coefficient in high-pressure superconducting hydrogen sulfide. Our results show that accounting for density effects improves the correlation between first-principles predictions and experimental measurements, specifically regarding the dependence of critical temperature on isotope mass and its variation with pressure.

Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concept of average excess, which effectively described the connection between a genetic trait and fitness, yet he distinguished between correlation and causation in his work. Although fitness has long been recognized as a causal factor, researchers often equate it with correlation in their studies. Similarly, modern scientists, relying on GWAS data, have recently proposed the Fundamental Lemma of Natural Selection, which in reality addresses a statistical association, or correlation, rather than a causal principle. Since no single variable can fully explain an organism's fitness and given that GWAS data fails to distinguish between an entity's causal traits and unchanging characteristics, both Fisher and the GWAS researchers, in their respective contexts, were able to identify the correlation they were measuring in their applications of their fundamental theories.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers ensure stable trajectories, we will analyze how feedforward push compensation combined with traditional slip recovery techniques, such as those based on trajectory tracking and recovery steps, interact with thruster-assisted walking. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we will evaluate the impact of parameter variations on completion rates, response times, and trajectory quality, specifically focusing on horizontal displacement. Moreover, we will investigate how utilizing thrusters influences these performance metrics, particularly in terms of bipedal robot stability and how parameter adjustments affect overall system stability. Ultimately, we will demonstrate that thruster-assisted walking achieves superior performance, resulting in faster response times and higher quality trajectories, resulting in more efficient movement and improved quality of gait.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering and matching 2D features with these entities. By leveraging machine learning-based descriptors, both speed and accuracy are significantly enhanced. A visual relocalization algorithm is developed using an attention mechanism to efficiently filter irrelevant features and optimize visualization efficiency. A surfel-based view synthesis module utilizing ray shooting technology is employed to accurately render novel views of a 3D scene. Experimental findings confirm the proposed method's superior performance in terms of view synthesis accuracy and relocalization error reduction when compared to existing image relocalization and synthesis approaches.

Decentralized learning technique, federated learning, protects user privacy while gathering data for training an AI model. Nonetheless, some users still share some data due to performance-versus-privacy trade-offs, making labeled data incomplete on the client side. Existing methods rely on full data sets from clients, making them unsuitable for partial labeling. This paper addresses the challenges of partial labeling in federated learning by utilizing quantized output features from unlabeled client data and cross-entropic regularization to synchronize these outputs with server-side class distributions. We use an unsupervised loss function that incorporates both classical and modern regularization techniques, such as contrastive loss, to enhance client model training in the absence of labels. We evaluate our proposed method through synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing it to existing approaches that make use of unlabeled client data. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method, outperforming the closest competitor by 4.52%, 2.5%, and 5.37% on Emotion线和, Sent140, and IMDB datasets respectively.

Simulations of binary black hole - neutron star merger events were performed over a broad range of parameters, including various locations of the initial neutron star, and different amounts of surrounding matter, and different amounts of surrounding matter, at different distances from the point of impact, and simulated events were carried out for approximately 0.5 seconds following the disruption of the neutron star.  Following the intense burst of gravitational radiation, there is a secondary, weaker signal caused by a massive accretion disk around the black hole, and this signal contains information about the position of the neutron star, and this position includes both the location and direction relative to the binary's angular momentum.  This secondary signal could provide a valuable way to cross-check measurements of this angular momentum.  While a neutron star at the ideal location produces a strong signal, other configurations still generate a detectable signal for certain distances, even as far as 10 megaparsecs.  These simulations suggest the presence of characteristic patterns in the signals from these events, and this research could lead to a greater understanding of the physical processes that occur during these merger events, and facilitate future studies of the early stages of ringdown motion, and the development of new methods of distinguishing between them.  This research could likely be utilized in future observed events, as it covers a broad range of neutron star masses, masses, and masses, and masses, and masses, and masses, and masses, and masses, and masses, and masses, and masses,

A novel variation of the Kawazumi-Zhang invariant, specifically $\varphi(C)$,
for compact Riemann surfaces $C$ of genus $g \geq 1$ is presented, exploring
its connections to the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class $e_1 = \kappa_1$ on the
moduli space and its relation to the traditional Kawazumi-Zhang invariant.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions.

This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near a graphene layer. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, we computed the optical force acting on each particle and derived equations to assess the influence of graphene's surface plasmons. Our findings demonstrate that the excitation of graphene's surface plasmons can produce numerous stable positions with interparticle distances much shorter than the photon wavelength. Additionally, we found that these positions can be dynamically manipulated by adjusting the graphene's chemical potential. Both perpendicular and angled light incidence have been taken into account in the study.

To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average treatment times using causal inference from observed data on 10,212 patients with abdominal pain in two New York City hospitals' emergency visits between 2012 and 2017. We treated length of stay as a continuous variable and found that extending Emergency Department treatment by one hour reduces admissions but increases hospitalizations the next day. Specifically, extending treatment time increases the admission rate from 30% to 38% and the hospitalization rate from 5% to 7.2% over a one-hour period. We also observed that extending treatment time has similar effects on both general and surgical patients, however the impact of admission process changes on these groups is not fully understood. We conclude that the apparent efficiency of longer Emergency Department visits may actually worsen patient outcomes by increasing hospitalization rates the next day.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents choose between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed among them. We develop a simple model of n agents, each requiring decision-making on which task to pursue, and explore how these decisions evolve into a strategic framework where there may be multiple pure-strategy Nash equilibria - situations where no agent can benefit from changing their task choice unilaterally. We establish that the number of such equilibria follows a bell-shaped distribution and increase in difficulty leads to the occurrence of mixed-strategy equilibria. This study has significant real-world implications, relevant to economic systems where agents make decisions on undertaking projects of varying risks and rewards.

Research has been conducted to analyze correlations caused by the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) between nucleons and charged particles in heavy-ion collisions through the ALICE experiment at top Fermi lab energies. The correlations examined include sub-event plane pairs, and the analysis revealed that one pair exhibited a stronger correlation than the other, with both showing the strongest effects in centrality ranges of 0-40% and 0-10% and per particle yields of 3.26, 0.67, 0.26, 0.13, 0.06, 0.02, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.

The surge in online crowdfunding platforms has transformed the act of funding projects into a prime example of interactive decision-making.  Researchers have become increasingly interested in understanding the factors that influence success in crowdfunding from a predictive perspective.  The current research contributes to this ongoing investigation by examining how funders' behavior signals affect projects' crowdfunding outcomes.  In contrast to traditional decision trees, researchers utilized regression analysis to investigate these influences, utilizing publicly available data on 17,000 projects from the Giggity platform in China.  They discovered that project presentation quality, goal setting accuracy, and funders' signaling behavior through existing funding amounts all contribute to project success.  Furthermore, they found that signaling behavior from funders plays a crucial role in determining which projects succeed, while also highlighting the importance of existing funding amounts in funders' behavior towards newly launched projects.

Developing machine learning networks to identify network attacks using a diverse range of data is complicated by multiple factors, including the need to integrate and clean data from varied sources and employ statistical analysis to eliminate anomalies and minimize discrepancies between datasets. Another issue is the lack of standardization in labeling data, which leads to inconsistent labeling practices and requires significant manual effort, resulting in time-consuming work and potential biases. In attempt to simplify this process, this research introduces a two-machine learning detection framework for network attacks, which can leverage data from multiple sources and use human feedback to leverage active learning techniques and minimize the number of required labeled instances.

This research focuses on creating an efficient real-time scheduling system for unoccupied mobile robots that can plan and execute a sequence of tasks. Our approach utilizes model-predictive control with multiple objectives, including time optimization, for planning and execution of these tasks. Due to varying dependencies and deadlines, some queries may necessitate immediate responses while others can be delayed. To address this, we develop a parallel scheduling algorithm using two data structures: one maps tasks to their corresponding robots for plan distribution, and the other tracks unfinished requests. A high-level process distributes planning among mobile robots, while a low-level mechanism moves completed but unscheduled queries to maintain system flow. Our results demonstrate that this method yields optimal schedules with significant model-free and dependency costs, along with bounds on schedule quality relative to ideal scenarios.

The performance of the interface between semiconductors and barriers plays a crucial role in producing quality qubits and efficient quantum wires. Our study investigates the characteristics of AlOx barriers on AlAs substrates using specific techniques, including high-purity materials and advanced measurement tools. These tools allow us to evaluate the quality of the interface by determining the level of impurities and the mobility of electrons. Our findings indicate that the semiconductors and barrier materials can be precisely matched, resulting in high mobility and low impurity levels at the interface. Additionally, we examine the performance of quantum devices fabricated from this type of material combination, focusing on charge transport and the stability of electrons used for quantum information storage. Our research demonstrates reliable and reproducible methods for creating AlOx barriers on AlAs, essential for improving the precision of quantum technology.

In complex networks, a phenomenon occurs where different clusters of oscillators, comprised of distinct systems, synchronize with their own distinct rhythms. When analyzing this complex synchronization pattern, we employ a linear stability analysis and identify stable limit cycles for each oscillator group. These distinct rhythms are then characterized using Lyapunov functions, but these functions lose their effectiveness when applied to systems with continuous symmetry. However, through our research, we develop universal Lyapunov functions, enabling the identification of synchronized frequency patterns across all groups, regardless of the system's symmetry level. These Lyapunov functions also facilitate the characterization of the system's stability, while our findings offer a systematic approach to understanding synchronization in systems comprising multiple balanced subsystems, while exploring the relationship between symmetry and stability.

Our study examines the existence of modality bias in visual search results when users perform cross-lingual searches. To achieve this, we measured the diversity of search outcomes across 11 major Western search engines, comparing them between queries posed in English and those translated into Spanish. These queries were selected from Datasets I2T and I2T-I2I of our search dataset search-multimodal-diversity, which consists of 1119 modal-matched image sets comprising English images and corresponding Spanish translations, all tagged with relevant tags, descriptions, captions, and related videos. To measure the diversity of search results, we calculated the API-call-based EE index for each search result set, considering the API-call costs when aggregating scores from different sources, including the Clip-Embedding API, YouTube-I2I API, and VSI-API. The analysis revealed that: (i) cross-lingual searches result in less diverse video outcomes, (i) IBERIA outperforms the competition in maintaining result diversity and (iii) combining the scores from YouTube, Vivino, and VSI significantly improves the overall result diversity.

To explore supersymmetric monodromy defects in the critical Wess-Zumino model to one-loop accuracy, researchers employed analytical bootstrapping techniques, breaking down the defect correlators into operator product expansion (OPE) blocks and solving the conformal bootstrap equations to derive constraints on their data. This process highlighted an issue with the theory's OPE coefficients and spectrum being affected by infinitesimally small parameters, making it impractical to determine the full theory data. Interestingly, this problem was found to be analogous in local theory data as well. Consequently, a modified program was proposed to regulate the theory's renormalization and further investigate the behavior of the defect under scale transformations. Additionally, researchers verified that the proposed program's results aligned with perturbation theory predictions for the anomalous dimensions of relevant operators, a finding also consistent with non-supersymmetric defects.

We prove that there is exactly one elliptic curve, up to uniqueness, defined over a cubic Galois field extension of rational numbers with a point on the curve having an order of 13 that is rational in the extension and that curve is not defined by the rational numbers.

The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, and its potential benefits in this context. In order to address this gap, we are studying the interference correlation, and its impact on the time it takes for a packet to experience a significant number of empty time slots in ad-hoc wireless networks. The focus of our research is on ALOHA-based packet transmission protocols, and we are comparing the interference correlation and its effect on delay under two scenarios: synchronous transmission protocols, where packet arrival times are coordinated with the active transmission intervals, and asynchronous transmission protocols, where packets are arrived without synchronization with the active transmission intervals. Our findings reveal that the long-term average delay decreases exponentially as the ratio of packet transmission intervals increases in the synchronous scenario, whereas in the asynchronous scenario, the long-term average delay decreases proportionally to this ratio. In addition, we are developing statistical properties of local delays, including their mean and variance under both scenarios, and observe that the gap between these properties decreases proportionally to the packet transmission intervals ratio as this gap continues to grow, confirming an empirical observation made earlier.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement a few available labels with high-confidence predictions made by the model on unlabeled nodes. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling approaches have shown limited success in this domain due to label noise. To address this scarcity of labels problem, we propose a novel informative pseudo-labeling framework. In each training iteration, we select the most informative pseudo-labels based on the model's confidence and then generate new unlabeled samples using label information to reinforce the model representation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially outperforms existing pseudo-labeling methods across multiple real-world datasets and graph structures.

In video processing tasks, spatial and spatio-temporal alignments are critically interconnected. Current approaches in patch or pixel feature learning utilize spatial information, disregarding temporal dimension, to space-alignment features. Contrary to conventional use of spatial information, this paper proposes leveraging temporal signals to generate space-aligned features. Experimental results demonstrate PEFNet, built upon this concept, significantly surpasses conventional approaches in video recognition tasks, achieving a substantial improvement of up to 6.2% over prominent momentum-based patch feature learning method, DPN, according to EPSTC benchmark.

We examine the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic boundaries, using parallel updating rules. To achieve this, we transform the process into a continuous-time master equation and apply a new transfer matrix method based on the T-matrix method commonly used in physics to study light propagation in multilayers. The transmission and reflection properties of the M-layer system are fully represented by the continuous-time transmission and reflection operators. By utilizing an identity operator and recursively decomposing the transmission operator, we break down the multi-layer problem into that of a single-layer system. The exact computation relies on the continuous eigenvalues and eigenfunctions previously found for the single-layer system's transmission operator. The associated reflection operator is determined through an integral expression involving the transmission operator's reflection components from adjacent layers. The calculation is supported by both theoretical analysis and numerical results, which align as the system's number of layers increases.

A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology from access points without the need for a signal-specific receiver, leverages underutilized frequency bands in the presence of noise. A mathematical model based on general information and power constraints allows for the simultaneous transmission of data and energy to mobile devices. The study investigates the beamforming design that optimizes either the data transmission rate or power transfer under various constraints. The results demonstrate the potential for more rapid data transmission and eco-friendly operation of mobile data networks, with practical validation provided by simulations.

We explored the magnetic property evolution of dilute Fermi gases with varying spin levels, observed alongside unitary transitions. Our analysis focused on non-interacting gas distributions, identifying emerging structures for gases with higher spin levels. To understand interactions, reduced wave functions were reduced to essential two-body components, allowing for the examination of asymptatic distribution swells as transitions occur. Furthermore, for levels above two, normalized spin levels were defined to quantify magnetic property evolution through fit parameters. These findings provide a framework for comparing bound state swells across different resonance types, including those not previously fully understood.

We introduce a simple, well-documented measurement method for determining minute mechanical oscillations in a parallel RLC circuit. The analysis centers on the RLC circuit paired with an electronically controlled capacitor, where the mechanical oscillator functions as a capacitor whose value changes in response to vibration. By utilizing RLC circuit components and standard electronic parts, our system achieves the necessary coupling between microwave fields and mechanical movements in microwave optomechanics. The coupling rate we obtain from this method aligns with that of superconducting lithographic optomechanical systems, while the approach remains applicable at room temperature. We demonstrate the technology using a set of RLC circuit components, achieving an average coupling rate of $6 \times 10^{-3}$ rad/s and a purity of signal $0.85 \times 10^{6}$ at 21 kHz band width. The simplicity and reliability of our technique make it suitable for applications in detecting minute movements in capacitive sensors, such as those in atomic force microscopes, while also serving as an educational tool in the context of advanced optomechanics.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

This study investigates how collective behavior and navigation skills develop in artificial agents governed by a fundamental rule: their movement responds to their proximity to obstacles, such that they approach when far away and retreat when close. To understand behavioral emergence, we created a novel visualization tool to track the development of individual agents' movement patterns and their impact on population activity over time. These artificial agents quickly learned to avoid barriers and, in confined spaces, their movement gave rise to coherent patterns: around corners, they would gather and create trails indicating the direction of flow, while in straight sections, their density would reveal areas of high concentration and accelerated movement. We demonstrated that our model can replicate key characteristics of active matter systems, suggesting a potential application for designing navigation agents with desired collective properties during their training.

This article explores and generalizes chiral aspects of Einstein's equations on two-dimensional spacetime with curvature.  We've extended the use of Bondi coordinates, originally applied to three-dimensional spacetime by Bondi, van der Burg, Rothstein, and Sasaki, with the chiral coordinates they employed. We've demonstrated that certain functions derived from the metric's components are inherently chiral as well. Unlike the relation between these functions in Einstein universality theory, we've discovered no formula that one can use to calculate non-singular, non-degenerate chiral coordinate transformations. We've examined how these transformations' singularities impact geodesics, specifically where the Jacobian's determinant vanishes or becomes infinite, and the significance of these transformations has on the stress-energy tensor.

Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view provided by the camera. Smoke generated from laser use in such operations obstructs visibility, necessitating smoke removal through a desmoking technique. This paper proposes an alternative approach to remove smoke without relying on external smoke suction. The method involves mapping smoke image features to distinguish smoke from tissue and separate layers of smoke using a depth information obtained through a simplified hidden Markov model. The technique has been successfully applied to laparoscopic surgery video frames, improving tissue visibility and overall visibility in medical procedures.

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions.

Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we have investigated two electrically neutral forms of barium titanate (BaTiO$_3$). To model the absence of charge, we adjusted the masses of ions based on their molecular weights in proportion to their actual masses. Our simulations of 1000 picoseconds each revealed that two theoretical structures accurately predict the known phase changes and physical properties of the material. These structures consist of atoms arranged in a uniform pattern and of a complex framework of repeating units. Predicted properties match with previous studies of the uniform pattern, while novel results have been obtained for the complex framework. Our findings suggest the use of classical simulations to model materials without electrical forces.

Multivariate data that involves functions over a defined range can be analyzed efficiently through Gaussian graphical models, specifically by capturing relationships within clusters of unrelated functional groups. This approach benefits from the increased sample sizes typically available in functional data analysis, which allows for substantial model customization. Furthermore, the techniques employed in our analysis are well-suited to the characteristics of functional data and can serve as a valuable tool for exploratory analysis and understanding data relationships. The method's precision and performance were evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrated its resilience to measurement errors and functional sample sizes. A real-world application involved analyzing functions representing spinal shapes over a defined range based on magnetic resonance imaging data from individuals in the UK, which helped to uncover relationships among different spinal clusters and size effects.

Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and currently unable to efficiently run the QAOA algorithm; to mitigate errors, the algorithm has been altered such that its objectives and constraints are formulated as a combination of Pauli operators. An algorithm called Pauli Alignment is proposed to find an optimized combination of these objectives and constraints in circuits comprising CNOT gates, resulting in substantially fewer weights than previously used approaches. In experiments, Pauli Alignment has been shown to consistently outperform the original QAOA algorithm on TSP instances, especially larger ones, in terms of execution time, number of alignments, and alignment quality. Notably, the method is able to function without alignments in most cases and matches the performance of existing solutions on these instances.

A new approach to analyzing Cox-Weyschweiler bounds offers insights into optimization problems. This approach not only bounds the condition number of certain problem classes, like those with DKK matrices, but also provides constraints on how many times an algorithm can exceed the optimal function value during iteration. Incorporating this new bound into an existing analysis of the CGMR method allows for a more precise prediction of its performance in relation to the eigenvalue concentration of a problem. This analysis reveals that most of the increase in the condition number of our theorems arises from potential deviations in eigenvalue distribution from the expected spectral density, and understanding these deviations can also help explain why some problems may not converge using the CGMR method.

Recent breakthroughs in manufacturing quality atomic layer deposition (ALD) van der Waals heterostructures have enabled researchers to delve into novel states within HgI$_2$ stacks, consisting of layers arranged in patterns such as A-B-A and A-B-A-B. An unexpected biexciton state forming from interactions between layers outside and inside the structure exhibits a binding energy of 400-500 microelectronvolts.

We introduce a machine learning-based method for determining location by leveraging mobile devices, which is particularly effective in areas with obstacles such as indoors. This approach utilizes mobile device sensors and signal data to predict the location of these devices more accurately, with particular focus on improving accuracy, reliability, and efficiency, with little to no latency. We apply this localization technique to various services and features, including mobile gaming, virtual reality, and remote vehicle operation, with a key application being distance estimation between two devices, such as for measuring the distance between players in mobile gaming or determining player movement in virtual reality and autonomous vehicle remote sensing. This approach accurately accounts for signal behavior, including reflection, diffraction, and refraction, with our system accurately capturing the relevant information in complex environments and efficiently localizing both fixed and moving devices, including two-way and one-way positioning methods, with high accuracy, reliability, and efficiency in real-time.

Measurements of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons in $W^{\pm}Z$ production have been reported, having been created in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, recorded by the ATLAS and CMS detectors in 2016.  Data totaling 138 fb$^{-1}$ in size were used to analyze joint $\rho$ angles between the $W$ and $Z$ bosons in the rest frame, according to the spin correlation $S_{CC}$, where $1$ signifies fully and $0$ indicates completely independent polarization states, resulting in a correlation value of $S_{CC}-1 = -0.123 \pm 0.017 \pm 0.009$, where the first error margin represents a statistical uncertainty, the second uncertainty represents a systematic error, and where a systematic error of 0.014 is estimated to result from the lack of knowledge about strong interaction.  Furthermore, it was observed that $WW$, $WZ$, and $ZZ$ cross sections, where both particles are fully transverse, total 0, and $S_{CC}$ values, where both particles are longitudinally polarised, total $1.16$, where both particles are in a $W$ longitudinal and $Z$ longitudinal state, where both particles total $0.64$, where both particles total $-0

Research indicates that the Cotton tensor offers a viable alternative to the Einstein equations, leading to new possibilities in general gravity theories and opening the door for a deeper understanding of gravitational black holes and thermodynamics. Furthermore, coupling a Cotton gravity term with topological descriptions has the potential to yield insights into charge distribution, as suggested by the law of conservation of charge derived from a non-trivial four-dimensional cohomology charge. We examine how the Cotton tensor and charge distribution behave in specific cases, including de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space-times, to gain a greater understanding of these complex concepts.

We've established a specific type of ordered relational topological space known as orthomodular spaces. Our method for creating these spaces involves combining a particular kind of frame, introduced by Hartonas, with a topology in a manner similar to the approach taken by Goldblatt and then extended by Bimbó, in relation to the representation theory of ortholattices. The orthomodular lattices and their corresponding homomorphisms can be shown to have a dual equivalence to the orthomodular spaces and their respective continuous morphisms.

We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats.

We demonstrate that the Riemann Hypothesis can be reduced to the validity of the Riemann zeta function's zero-reduction conjecture for holomorphic Hecke cusp forms whose eigenvalues are constrained to a narrowly defined interval. This in turn implies the validity of the Lorentzian Riemann Hypothesis.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for IPM preconditioning often neglect the residual of the preconditioned residual, leading to unnecessary computations. This paper presents an interior point method that utilizes a novel termination criterion for IPM preconditioning, devoid of any interior point algorithm-specific parameters. Despite not using the coarser components, our proposed criterion outperforms in performance, providing a significant reduction in computation time of around 2-3 times.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass scenarios in the Larin scheme.
Furthermore, the result serves as a crucial transition function for the variable
flavor number scheme at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ and is also expressed in momentum
space for convenient use.

Established industries such as aviation gather real-life mistakes in centralized databases to facilitate safer practices. Despite the immense potential of similar efforts for emerging intelligent systems, no comprehensive and publicly accessible repositories of failures exist yet. To address this gap, we introduce IR-IKI, a Google Forms-based system designed to collect informed consent user submissions of intelligent system-related incidents. By selecting appropriate descriptors, our system streamlines data collection and organizes a dataset with documented incident details, corresponding descriptive labels, and a categorized taxonomy. The built-in data analysis features facilitate understanding of incident patterns and automatically update the taxonomy. A primary focus of our research involves the automated taxonomy creation, guided by an extended Merkle tree, where incident descriptions are linked to corresponding taxonomy branches for seamless integration. By analyzing 315 collected automation incidents, we developed a taxonomy with five criteria and twenty categories, then compared the chosen taxonomy with an alternative one to evaluate their effectiveness. Furthermore, we evaluated a method to link incident data with taxonomy structures, finding IR-IKI to be a practical tool for dynamic taxonomy management.

The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. To generalize this connection in Yang--Mills theory while maintaining gauge invariance, we propose an ERG equation based on a similarity principle and further extend it to lattice gauge theory from the continuum theory context.

Current business process monitoring methods mainly concentrate on extracting a process model from historical data, however this approach presents challenges when real-world data is used due to complex variations and additional data sources like electronic health records that can reveal which guidelines were actually followed. Building upon this, we introduce the Medical Process Compliance Monitoring approach that aims to monitor how well specified medical processes are followed. This method considers both the available medical guidelines and real data on process compliance in areas like clinical treatment and diagnosis. As obtaining this real-world data can be challenging or unethical, we developed a partnership with a medical institution that allowed us access to data extracted from patients' records. This led us to identify four key issues with the available data and propose solutions to address these problems.

Quipper, a domain-specific language, facilitates quantum circuit construction through functional programming concepts. Building on this foundation, we develop linear lambda calculus with recursion and propose Qlambda, a linear functional language for quantum programming. We establish a connection between the two by deriving a lambda calculus from Qlambda's semantics, then demonstrate that both Qlambda and an existing quantum programming language, Quil, describe the same quantum circuits. Furthermore, we show that the lambda calculus is typable under certain conditions, including proper ordering of qubits and classical bits. We introduce quantum types with reference capabilities, enabling the representation of measured classical bits. We develop a core type theory with substantial logical metatheory, including structural operational semantics, subject expansion and substitution, and subject reduction, together with a strong normalization result. We establish that the lambda calculus, quantum machines, and a basic machine model all describe the same quantum circuits, and prove that the lambda calculus is coherent by constructing a functional mapping between quantum circuits and their interpretations in a quantum category.

In this study, we have modelled a two-dimensional percolation model using random matrices with asymmetric variance, where we found that an eigenvalue splitting phenomenon occurs above a critical threshold, where four extreme eigenvalues converge to a constant value. Through a circular domain expansion, we have evaluated the impact of this eigenvalue splitting on the model's critical behavior, and our results suggest that the transition is continuous and occurs at a point where the control parameter equals zero. Additionally, we found that critical exponents vary depending on the degree of asymmetry in the model, where we have estimated the range in which the transition remains unchanged and occurs abruptly.

We suggest creating bosonic pairs using large numbers of dipoles with complex internal structures, which interact with an isolated optical cavity. A rapid growth of entanglement between these dipoles arises from the virtual exchange of photons, resulting in early signs of thermalization within this confined system. However, by utilizing dipoles with intricate internal structures, we can significantly enhance this pair-bothing effect. In our proposed setup, we use warm rubidium atoms and an optical cavity, where two of these atoms' internal states Bothing two modes of light and atoms. While this rapid growth of entanglement typically signifies loss of coherence, we demonstrate how the complex internal structure can maintain coherence and enhance entanglement through simultaneous absorption and emission of multiple photons.

Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a complex computational problem with not-one-size-fits-all solution due to varying read lengths and coverages across genomes. High-quality long-read genomics tools have been lacking for efficient genome assembly on scalable cloud platforms. To address this issue, we introduce GenotypeGenome, cloud-ready tool for genome assembly optimized for varying read lengths, designed to deliver accurate results across different genomes. GenotypeGraph, core algorithm of GenotypeGenome, constructs a compact representation of overlapping sequences, thereby streamlining memory usage and efficiency. Utilizing a graph-based model, we then perform precise operations to accurately reconstruct genomes. GenotypeGenome is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/psu-bioinfo/GenotypeEngine.

A modified logistic equation, previously known as Hutchinson's equation, failed to provide a plausible framework for explaining oscillating populations within its original context. Researchers now propose an alternative application, primarily applicable to discrete-time models representing population dynamics. They argue that, although improbable, the equation could be validly representable as continuous-time processes under a unique set of conditions. One such example involves the analysis of red-backed shrike breeding success over a 50-year period, which shows a notable decline beginning in the late 20th century. Additionally, it is indicated that other logistic-based equations might require similar, counterintuitive interpretations.

The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be applied to temporal point processes for measuring the regularity or typical characteristics of their intensity functions. We have developed a time-based depth approach that involves solving a linear programming problem for estimating the depth of these intensity functions. Our approach has been thoroughly tested using 100 synthetic and real-world examples, which revealed its regularity and robustness. As a practical application of our methodology, we have created a way to determine the most significant intensity functions within a group, which can be utilized in defining density regions or clustering these intensity functions.

Achieving maximum engine performance involves leveraging quantum effects. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing a broader range of tasks and (2) minimizing irreversible losses inherent in thermal converters. In classical four-node heat engines, we demonstrate that quantum systems can be designed to avoid losses and enhance performance through frequency tuning, equivalent to increasing conductivity in classical devices. Findings suggest that simpler methods for enhancing engine performance correlate with more feasible quantum advantages.

Researchers employed a precise laser spectroscopy method on three isotopes of germanium at the ISOLDE-CERN facility to study their hyperfine properties. The measurements involved a highly accurate laser source with a 269 nm wavelength, generated through a combination of techniques, and were detected using a combination of detector types. The study included a significant improvement in understanding the nuclear quadrupole moments and moments of $^{67}$Ge and $^{69}$Ge for the first time, and verified the quadrupole moment of $^{68}$Ge with increased accuracy. The results led to refined isotopic mass estimates for $^{67}$Ge and $^{69}$Ge, and supported the investigation of the potential violation of fundamental symmetries, such as the conversion between protons and neutrons.

A novel method for accurately measuring the masses of extremely short-lived, exotic atomic particles has been developed and implemented at the Isolde facility of the European Council for Nuclear Research. The Isolation in Storage Ion Cyclotron Resonance technique allows for the precise analysis of rare, short-lived ions by exploiting their behavior in a magnetic field. Using this method, researchers have obtained the first mass measurements of a specific range of selenium isotopes and verified selected results with exceptional accuracy, semi-relativistically, expanding upon traditional methods.

This tutorial notebook demonstrates a Monte Carlo simulation technique for lattice field theories using Python, exemplified by the Ising model. It builds upon the second edition of "Lectures on Lattice Field Theory" by Creutz, incorporating modern methods such as vectorized and vectorized code written in Python.

We aim to enhance the accuracy of structured text recognition by incorporating predefined formats defined through regular expressions, thereby facilitating the identification of specific patterns. Our method, involving a Weighted Finite-State Transducer model, boosts recognition accuracy on targeted formats, with minimal losses in other instances. A key parameter governs the intensity of the formatting constraints, enabling a gradual transition from general recognition to format-based recognition. Experimental findings demonstrate improved performance on tagged German text datasets, with open-source availability of our Weighted Finite-State Transducer system and associated software.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks in association with the Higgs boson through the Higgs boson decaying into two photons, an process analyzed in data collected at 13 TeV with a total luminosity of 137 fb-1.  A multi-variable analysis utilizing Deep Neural Networks was carried out to enhance signal significance beyond traditional methods, resulting in a significant increase in the signal-to-background ratio.  With a statistical power of 11.6 sigma, a significant deviation from Standard Model expectations was identified, with a significant statistical shift of 2.6 (sigma) in the signal cross-section for top quark production in association with the Higgs boson decaying into two photons.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe changes and develops. Although only 10% of the sky is covered in the LoTSDR1 J2000 data release, preliminary analysis of the LoTSDR1 data has yielded valuable information on the radio sources within the sky and how their numbers vary. With the publication of the LoTSDR2 data, new data was added to existing databases to enhance the accuracy of measurements related to the population of radio sources in the sky and how their numbers vary. By utilizing the Cross-Matched LoTSDR2 Cross-Matched catalog, the model of the population is refined and slightly altered. Calculations of abundance indices for three different frequency bands reveal that the population model in the high-density limit is not uniform across different frequency bands and that there is a notable difference between the models for 107, 142 and 230 MHz.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. However, the original HDR Lasso problem is non-convex and difficult to resolve. A new, computationally tractable HDR Lasso problem is formulated using the Lasso regression model. A proximal point method is suggested, and its linear convergence rate is proven. An implemented software, Rdr, has been developed, and a comprehensive framework for HDR Lasso problem formulation is provided, including variable selection and semi-supervised dimension reduction models. All models are efficiently solved by the proposed proximal point method, which demonstrates robust results on various numerical experiments.

Identifying whether an optimal solution is localized or universal is particularly challenging when the solution involves minimizing a complex functional. To address this challenge, this study demonstrates that for any system that can be efficiently simulated, if the functional is complex optimization problem, any small improvement from an existing protocol will also be optimal, this study demonstrates that for any optimal protocol that cannot further be improved locally, it will also be optimal globally. To demonstrate the applicability of this method, it is successfully applied to the case of optimal protocols for minimizing entropy production, where any optimal protocol that cannot further be improved locally, it will also be optimal globally.

Over the past decade, significant advancements have been made in artificial intelligence, particularly in leveraging AI to address environmental concerns such as air quality monitoring and energy efficiency. This paper delves into how AI can be used to tackle environmental challenges, but more importantly, it sheds light on the potential adverse effects of AI-driven environmental solutions, which have received relatively little attention to date. Through a systematic literature review, the paper identifies and categorizes methods for AI to address environmental issues, as well as approaches to mitigate any negative environmental impacts AI may have. By synthesizing recent findings from across diverse research disciplines, the paper provides a comprehensive overview of how AI can be employed to benefit the environment, as well as necessary measures to prevent any potential harm caused by AI technologies. Ultimately, the paper aims to foster greater awareness of AI's role in both addressing and being affected by environmental concerns, as well as promoting responsible AI development that adequately considers environmental implications.

This paper investigates and classifies various prescriptive process monitoring methods, focusing on their capacity to identify recommended actions for process operators in order to achieve predefined process goals.
