In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms forming a chain, with some ruideum atoms

Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) have garnered significant interest for their ability to efficiently model images and videos; nevertheless, using separate networks for each frame in a video sequence can be computationally costly. We explore whether a unified network can simultaneously represent a whole video and a single frame without compromising performance, finding that this approach does yield comparable results. We further develop a novel dual-network architecture that processes both frame-level details and temporal information, enabling more targeted parameter allocation and enhanced representation efficiency. We apply this framework to various video processing tasks, including feature extraction, conditional generation, and end-to-end video synthesis, and achieve significant memory reduction while attending to relevant video segments without any performance loss or training overhead.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either domain classification or adaptation of decision boundaries. We enhance these approaches by integrating them with semi-supervised learning, enabling the full utilization of unlabelled domain data in co-operation with semi-supervised pseudo labels. Consequently, semi-supervised learning becomes a viable option even significant domain data is available. We evaluate two open-source unlabelled adaptation modules, a domain classifier and an entropy classifier, along with two semi-supervised learning methods, for image classification in the face of substantial domain shift. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on three extensive image datasets, Top-10-MNIST, MNIST-REMBER and VisA-EMBER, demonstrating that semi-supervised adaptation yields substantial performance improvements over its supervised counterpart, especially in domains with large shift values. We also expose a vulnerability in current adaptation modules, showing that they can mislead the learning process by selecting easy samples for adaptation. These samples have minimal contribution to classification accuracy, but negatively impact CDA through its neural network re-initialization process. We validate that incorporating GMM-based CBA and DBM as robust alternative unlabelled adaptation modules, along with semi-supervised learning, can yield excellent classification results with significantly reduced standard deviation in the same setting.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric framework for deep learning models by identifying their respective manifolds and tangent spaces. Building on this, we introduce a novel dynamic representation for system trajectories, and examine how different optimization strategies behave within this geometric context. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to quantum neural networks, comparing their geometric properties to those of classical neural networks.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ Lattice $L$, focusing on the application of Szpiro's algorithm for computing generator rings of this lattice minimum sequence. Specifically, we investigate the application of the minimum sequence's first two elements, $a$ and $b$, in the context of Szpiro's algorithm. Our results demonstrate that the pair $(a,b)$ generates an ambiguous principal ideal if and only if the ideal generated by $b$ factorizes into prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_1,\ldots,\mathfrak{p}_g$ where each $\mathfrak{p}_i$ factorizes into rational prime ideals $\mathfrak{q}_{i,1},\ldots,\mathfrak{q}_{i,h_i}$ such that the $\mathfrak{q}$s are fourth powers and their exponents are all divisible by four.

A research framework is introduced to investigate deep neural network classifiers for state-of-the-art jet substructure techniques. This technique involves training a single network classifier across multiple methods, which rely on different expert variables specifically crafted for each method. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated by achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art single-network classifiers, but through collaborative action of multiple specialized neural networks. Furthermore, the study reveals that increasing the number of expert variables enhances accuracy within a diminishing range, indicating the potential for collaborative problem solving among multiple neural networks.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient calculation of relevant physical characteristics, thanks to its symbolic composition using non-Abelian cosets. This approach leveraged symbolic computation tools to establish the transformation properties of wave functions defined at specific points within a crystal's fundamental unit.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure, organized as torus bundles over simple simply-connected, positively curved manifolds, or, in the case of non-compact manifolds, constructed from flat factors and compact, positively curved manifles.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, we explore how to implement a natural mechanism for baryon generation. $U(1)_B$ gauge symmetry, derived from the free baryon number, is considered, with its origin linked to the xiton field's $B-L$ symmetry, which is protected by discrete $Z_8$ symmetry and broken by higher-dimensional operators.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that defines their operational principles and subsequent influences on users, followed by a classification of current VPPMs and their applications, then proceeding to identify ways in which VPPMs can be manipulated to mislead users. A particular focus is given to discussing ethical considerations when VPPMs are used to influence human behavior and presenting initial findings from relevant empirical studies. The paper concludes by presenting a roadmap for further investigation into VPPMs, emphasizing the pressing need to understand their potential threats to user safety and privacy, and enhancing VR interactivity in a responsible manner.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and NOEMA data on a low-mass core in the process of forming stars, labeled L1521ES, have revealed two distinct binary fragments. We have used precise imaging to accurately determine the core's mass and the location, mass, and separation of the fragments. Based on this information, we have also used simulations to estimate the properties of the central fragment and the mass of the binary system. Our analysis indicates that the core's mass distribution is fairly symmetrical, with the majority of the mass collected by the central fragment. The degree of mass asymmetry also depends on the total mass of the parent core, being less pronounced in higher-mass cores. Furthermore, the binary fragments' mass and separation are correlated, exhibiting lower masses at larger separations. Our study suggests that the binary fragments' mass and separation are also dependent on the total core mass, the total core mass placing a ceiling on the mass of the binary fragments, with a predicted maximum mass of approximately 0.25 solar masses for a 1 solar mass core. The binary fragments' mass also decreases with increasing separation, likely due to the increased influence of the core's rotating disk, which also decreases with increasing separation.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness is limited by the influence of kernel parameters. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach utilizes a fastrICA algorithm on a transformed space from kernel projection to minimize dimensionality and maximize information content while reducing data points impacted by noise and extreme data values. Various kernel functions, including Gaussian, uniform, and linear, were considered along with arcsinh transformations. They were implemented with three different algorithms to identify key features from high-dimensional data. Unlike ICA, FastICA provides several advantages over existing methods due to its computational efficiency, flexibility, and noise tolerance, except for the effect on distorted data values. Unlike other transformations, the proposed arcsinh transformation significantly reduces the influence of extreme data values. By combining FastICA with arcsinh transformation, the proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach improves feature extraction from random data more effectively, especially in high-dimensional datasets affected by noise and extreme data values. Furthermore, the proposed method was tested using simulated and real-world datasets with significant results and was shown to outperform existing methods in identifying features from datasets impacted by noise and extreme data values.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. Researchers have long known that certain properties of graphs can be identified in polynomial time within polynomial calculus and choiceless polynomial time. This link allows us to draw similar conclusions about the extended polynomial calculus with bounded degrees. Specifically, we explore the implications of extending graphs with random functional inputs, known as functional augmentation. By analyzing these functional inputs, we establish a connection between proving properties of augmented graphs and finding short witnesses in these graphs, regardless of the degree bound. Furthermore, we show that extended polynomial calculus with bounded degrees and some additional linear inputs can identify non-isomorphic graphs, resolving a long-standing question in finite model theory. This breakthrough also has graph isomorphism tests as significant applications.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection exists, the ring covering number $\sigma(R)$ in $R$ is determined by the cardinality of a minimal collection, and a ring is $\sigma$ elementary when $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for any ideal of $R$, given it is non-zero, two sided and in $R$. The given text describes the discovery of first ring $\sigma$ elementary instances which possess non-trivial Jacobson radical $J$  and a ring that is non commutative in $R/RJ$, while determining ring covering numbers in various rings such as certain non commutative groups $G$, and in polynomial rings $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_m]/(g_1,\ldots,g_k)$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on various topics. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we introduce CLARIFY, a semantic approach to fact-checking that utilizes synonymy and antonymy relations. By understanding the context and structure of arguments, our method can assess their credibility and identify inconsistent or implausible information. By combining semantic similarity with argument analysis, CLARIFY emerges as a promising technique for assessing the accuracy of complex content and pinpointing areas of discrepancy.

Social media platforms like Twitter provide real-time data streams that allow us to anticipate major events such as protests, earthquakes, and elections. However, accessing these platforms directly can be costly, making it essential to design data gathering strategies that enable prediction while minimizing costs. In this paper, we introduce a framework for directing data acquisition processes to produce accurate real-world event predictions. This framework is grounded in semantic event detection, a approach that involves recognizing and understanding relationships between events. We represent this model as a directed acyclic graph, where nodes depict events and edges represent relationships such as simultaneity, divergence, and succession. We then formulate a data acquisition optimization problem, aiming to identify the most informative data points within this model to accurately detect events. This problem is posed as a maximization of information gain under a budget constraint, and we propose a greedy strategy to utilize mutual information for event detection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations of actual Twitter data streams related to the Syrian civil war.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurement and tomographic galaxy surveys offer fresh opportunities for analyzing the sky on large scales with precise efficiency. We developed an effective method to determine galaxy bias and the power spectrum of cosmic structures using the weighted skew-spectrum ($S_1^{\rm post}$), which captures non-Gaussian information in galaxy distribution data beyond conventional power spectra. By utilizing the cosmology-independent $S_1^{\rm post}$, we analyzed data from cosmic tomography obtained from the Cosmicflows-3 database, which includes redshift and dipole data on galaxies up to $z \approx 2.5$. Initial results application of our model to only a subset of the available data revealed the evolution of cosmic structure parameters without relying on pre-set assumptions, yielding an estimated value of the distance to the last dynamical horizon ($d_H$) of approximately $2.58 \times 10^{27}$ cm and suggesting a parameter ratio in a cosmic model to be approximately $0.307$, consistent with results from the Pantheon sample and equivalent to a Hubble constant of approximately $69.4$ km/Mpc when paired with a cosmic density parameter of about $0.307$. It ultimately proved possible to accurately analyze all available galaxy data within the specified redshift range through our approach, which might enable us to constrain cosmic structure parameters with surprising precision.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic caused widespread disruption, and a related rumor crisis spread rapidly across the internet, making urgent cross-platform rumor verification necessary. Existing research into rumor detection has primarily relied on a single platform or a few methods, making multi-source rumor verification with advanced techniques scarce. This study presents a novel framework for cross-platform rumor detection. To effectively analyze virtual accounts, hidden graph structures, and dispersed online rumors, we developed the XCD model, which combines edge-conditioned model recurrent neural networks and multi-source rumor features. By reconstructing user relationship graphs from multiple platforms, extracting keyword information, and using an edge-conditioned model to classify rumors, XCD achieves superior online rumor detection performance. Experimentally, XCD outperformed existing methods, and our dataset and XCD implementation are publicly available.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality on classification performance using four diverse datasets in underground mining, a pioneering field for hyperspectral applications. Each dataset was compressed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Competitive Collaborative Subspace Projection (CCSP) to analyze optimization opportunities and evaluate various algorithms. The research employed six classification algorithms and evaluated them across compression rates from 10 to 500. The outcomes illustrate how varying compression levels affect classification accuracy and reveal a optimal compression threshold beyond which performance gains diminish, contradicting the conventional belief that higher compression rates always lead to better classification results.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within these networks, however, remains elusive. In search of a viable mechanism, researchers discovered that trainability can be utilized to dissect network components into distinct parts, concurrently highlighting the existence of sub-networks that can be trained effectively after removing other components. "The lottery ticket hypothesis" posits that these sub-networks constitute the essential information content of neural networks. We present an algorithm that identifies these sub-networks through iterative "winning lottery ticket extraction" and demonstrate its efficacy by showing that our generated tickets consistently achieve comparable accuracy to the full-network model on CIFAR-10 after being trained using minimal parameters.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with experiments, combining protein and peptide datasets with massive quantum calculations, resulting in highly accurate predictions within milliseconds per residue, far exceeding traditional methods in speed and precision and meeting the requirements of experiments with proteins and complexes.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as crucial in creating robust models. Despite loss functions being essentially articulated prior to execution, current deep learning frameworks enable their modification during training through automatic differentiation. This research investigates how changing the loss function at various points during training affects subsequent performance. By conducting loss functions ablation study on standard datasets, it was discovered that, contrary to intuition, the optimal loss function is often best suited towards the end of training rather than being most impactful at the beginning.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting particles is a long-standing and difficult challenge in physics. One novel approach for improving the understanding of these systems is parquet theory. Developed in the 1960s, this approach focuses on pairwise interactions but struggles to account for the limitations of its application to higher-order processes. Researchers have tested the parity of the approximation in various systems. However, its applicability to superfluid $^4$He has been limited to the examination of elementary excitations. This study extends the application to static, long-wavelength properties. One such property is the superfluid fraction, another is the static dielectric susceptibility, and a third is the long-wavelength speed of sound. Results demonstrate that the parity of the approximation fails at very short wavelengths or low temperatures. However, its failure is intricate, involving the interplay between the system's length scales and energy characteristics. Parity's shortfalls can be remedied using an enhanced approximation that involves four-boson effects. This corrected approach aligns seamlessly with the system's low-energy, long-wavelength behavior, including the emergence of a nearly conformal regime in sound velocity at low temperatures.

The process of exciton condensation is theorized to occur when bound electron-hole pairs spontaneously undergo a phase transition. This phenomenon has primarily been studied in excitonic insulators through light absorption techniques, but this method's sensitivity to both electrons and holes makes it challenging to isolate the excitons. To overcome this limitation, we developed an innovative approach that utilizes nonlinear magnetization contrast imaging of a magnetic exciton, leveraging its solely electron-like response via spin resonance in zero magnetic field. This technique allows us to map the spatial distribution of excitons, providing valuable insights into their behavior. Additionally, we observed the growth of exciton density under increasing light intensity, as well as the development of a circular domain pattern around a defect site at high excitation levels, providing direct evidence of the radial flow of excitons. This finding agrees with simulations based on a drift-diffusion model. Furthermore, we observed gradient exciton-induced semiconductor-to-insulator spin-splitting changes, suggesting a starting point for the study of topological properties of magnetic excitonic insulators.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted digital reporting systems to allow users to submit incident reports directly to community safety teams, similar to traditional non-emergency call centers. Despite the benefits of these platforms, their effectiveness in ensuring timely and accurate report submission has been limited by user confusion and frustration over technical difficulties. Therefore, we investigated the impact of emotional support provided by customer service representatives, known as dispatchers, on user engagement with these systems. Through analyzing a dataset of over 55,000 community safety reporting records from San Francisco, we developed a framework to measure community-submitted incident quality and quantity. Our results demonstrate that dispatchers play a pivotal role in enhancing both the volume and standard of community-submitted safety reports. Notably, communities receiving greater emotional support from dispatchers exhibited lower rates of duplicate report removal, higher average report submission rates, and more diverse demographic representation in submitted reports. These findings suggest that dispatchers' emotional support leads to increased report submission rates, reduced technical difficulties, and improved report diversity. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of valuing dispatchers' emotional support as a key factor in powering community safety technologies.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with Mg atoms, we investigate the magnetic field's effect on match-mismatch conditions, critical currents, and other properties of type-N and type-II superfluids in this material. We calculate the thermodynamic properties of two models - the pseudospin Fermi model and the Dirac model - and determine the Gibbs free energy for both in the thermodynamic limit. A key aspect of our analysis is understanding the influence of matching magnetic field H$_c1$ and critical H$_c2$ surface states have on the Gibbs free energy, resulting in distinct outcomes based on whether the superfluid is of the N or II type. Additionally, we compute the specific heat of both models and observe that it exhibits a linear temperature dependence at low temperatures regardless of whether the superfluid is of the N or II type. Ultimately, our comparison with experimental specific heat results on two samples of magnetically-doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ indicates that the match-Majorana superfluid is of the N type, while the Dirac superfluid displays characteristics of type-II with H$_{c2}$ being anisotropic, consistent with experimental observations of resistance drops under specific magnetic field orientations.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, informative instances to be annotated by human operators. Present techniques either evaluate pre-trained models' uncertain outputs or assess the differences in pre-trained and re-trained models with varying labels. From a theoretical standpoint, the latter approach is justified through the relationship between information and mutual dependence. Nevertheless, the quality of multiple annotations impacts model uncertainty more rapidly than data intrinsic properties. Therefore, the paper investigates and illustrates, through annotation quality and entropy, sample selection based on both entropy and the quality of multiple annotations. We evaluate the proposed approach on image description generation across multiple datasets.

To study how music changes over time, we analyze the global popularity of over 760,000 songs from 1958 to 2020. We focus on two characteristics of music: loudness complexity and danceability. Surprisingly, we discover that popular songs exhibit patterns similar to creative writers, where each new song builds upon previous ones while introducing unique elements. Our analysis reveals significant transformations in music style since the 1960s, with distinct changes in loudness complexity, songs becoming louder and more energetic. Additionally, we observe an increase in songs' danceability since 2000, leading to the conclusion that popular music style today differs from last century, much like writers in music today differ from those of last century.

A novel category of stochastic processes that combine reinforcement and growth dynamics is studied, where the probability of a new number either starting a new block or joining an existing one depends on that block's size through separate functions. This paper derives exact mathematical expressions for key statistical measures, including the distribution of block sizes, and uses asymptotic analysis to gain additional insights. Notably, when specific functions related to the process are considered as functions of a variable 's', they often lead to the same type of difference equations, enabling the application of similar solution methods.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions - internal stability and internal decomposition - previously introduced by Asperti.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through learning a state space clustering model, we automatically assign comparatives to appropriate regions, thereby enhancing labeling accuracy and leading to a substantial decrease in required human labels. We present our approach in this paper and demonstrate its effectiveness through careful experimentation. Specifically, our method achieves a 10x reduction in required human labels over existing methods while maintaining performance on par with them.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We explore singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are utilized to establish a novel family of solutions in 2D ideal magnetohydrodynamics that maintain constant vorticity and magnetic field strength. These solutions in MHD are analogous to a specific class of ideal fluid dynamical solutions originally developed in the study of pointed vortex loops. The magnetohydrodynamical applications are extensively explored with a focus on the dynamic behavior of loop-like structures within the system.

Under specific conditions, the augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) estimator and its neighboring AIPW estimator (nAIPW) estimator exhibit similarities. Both estimators possess the characteristics of being doubly robust and consistent, with nAIPW also displaying asymptotic bias reduction and enhanced efficiency in the case of binary treatments. The nAIPW estimator's performance outshines that of AIPW through a testable inequality, and two implementations of nAIPW are explored: a general implementation with AIPW and its simplified counterpart for locally constant treatments.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in weak decays, which is potentially a sign of new physics. Given the enhanced sensitivity of hadron colliders to $\tau$-related signals compared to its lighter counterparts, the $B$ factory experiments have a limited capacity to explore this area in contrast to the LHCb and Belle II experiments. This paper discusses various experimental techniques for $\tau$ signal detection at the B factory, focusing on the $\tau$'s distinctive decay products and their mass difference from the $\mu$ and $e$ particles, enabling signaling of rarer processes such as $\mu\to e$ conversions. The paper also examines $\tau$ production at muon beams and how their decays could provide insights into both known and uncommon couplings beyond the Standard Model.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to analyze the general circulation on a global scale in real-time at lab facilities, offering a detailed and observable representation of atmospheric phenomena.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using fewer parameters than TREND model fits, it requires selecting an optimal threshold. Lower thresholds result in more parameter estimates but fewer super-threshold events, whereas higher thresholds yield more uniform parameter estimates but are prone to including events influenced by model misspecification. Introducing a single threshold-independent parameter vector in a new TREND model can resolve this dilemma. Estimation relies on constructing likelihood functions based on two types of transformed variables above the threshold: their minimum values and spacings between consecutive extremes. These minimum values and spacings above the threshold have known Generalized Extreme Value distributions with distinct location and scale parameters, respectively, allowing for efficient TREND model estimation via a Bayesian approach utilizing a relational model and the principle of noninformative relative densities. The approach was evaluated using simulation studies of real data modelling, including daily UK general temperature and hourly Amazon river water levels.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that arises when only the state-action reward tuple database is available, without necessarily reflecting the true environmental dynamics. Our research develops robust policy reinforcement algorithms that guarantee a certain level of performance degradation relative to the optimal policy, based on the assumptions that adversaries modify only a limited fraction of the database tuples and possibly a limited bandwidth for additional information. Our key findings include an algorithm with polynomial complexity, where performance degradation is directly proportional to the adversary's modification bandwidth. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis identifies the minimal amount of data required to learn the optimal policy, taking into consideration the adversary's constraints. Our findings open up numerous avenues for further research in offline reinforcement learning.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison.

Artificial molecular motors have the potential to generate mechanical work through mass transport driven by electric currents. As a result, the design of these motors is heavily influenced by the electric currents. To better understand this relationship, researchers applied first-principles calculations to investigate the electric current profiles of two types of molecules: artificial motors and natural motors. They found that the mechanical structure of artificial motors contributes significantly to their anomalous currents. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of currents at later stages favors mechanical motion. This finding suggests that the mechanism behind their operation may involve electric mass transfer rather than the traditional mass conservation principle.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios.

We begin by exploring the straightforward method for calculating the $f$-Convolution between two functions, $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$, and determine its time complexity, which is $\mathcal{O}(n^{3})$.  Next, we consider a specific case where the set $\Lambda$ in the $\Lambda$-restricted $f$-Convolution contains a constant number of elements, and we analyze its time complexity, which results in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\max\{|\Lambda|,|\mathbb{A}|\}\cdot\log n)$.  Then, we introduce two key concepts: commutative functions and equivalence relations associated with them, enabling us to consider a convolution operation on the set of equivalence classes.  This leads to the definition of cosets and their properties, including composition and a connection to a group structure when the function is commutative.  Finally, we examine the $f$-Convolution for functions with a finite domain and an abelian group for the set $\mathbb{A}$, introducing the concept of a support for a function and its restriction to the set of non-zero elements.  This allows for a revised definition of $f$-Convolution, which is closed under a binary operation denoted by $*$.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1996 led to ongoing debates about its classification due to differing interpretations from initial spectroscopic data analysis. Despite GJ 229B being one of the most extensively studied T-dwarfs, our understanding of its spectrum has relied mostly on comparison-based fits and template spectroscopy, which have often produced inconsistent results. Given GJ 229B's extensively explored nature, its classification remains crucial for testing and comparing effective temperature (Teff) and mass (Mass) range estimates from existing and future dwarf research. Utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data from 0.6-13.5 micrometers obtained from multiple telescopes, our study for the first time applies simultaneous L, T, and water vapor (H2O) line retrievals using the LAP-Code to determine the atmospheric composition of GJ229B. Our analysis yields a mass range of 25-95 Jupiter masses and a Teff range of 650-950 K, and may provide further insights into the atmospheric composition of GJ229B by potentially verifying the presence of methane and titanium oxide as well as ruling out pure water vapor atmospheres.

We explore the possible network of reactions involving an unusual state, specifically the pions, and calculates how it would affect the decay of $\rho$ mesons, all within the framework of tetraquarks. By considering two different models, one where the state has the properties of $0^{++-}$ and another where it has $0^{++-}$, and applying principles related to reaction symmetry and the flow between different state forms, we compare our calculations with current experimental data using statistical measures, $\chi^2$. Our analysis points towards an $I^YJ=\tfrac12^-{\rm Y}=0$ state, below $2$ GeV, where we detect pions attached to $\rho$ mesons, applying processes influenced by anomalous higher-order symmetry. In the process, we find that, below $2$ GeV, there may be no state with the properties of $C=P=+$ and $Y=0$.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_\phi$ and width difference $\Delta A$ of the $B_s^0$ meson by studying $B_s^0\to J/\psi K^+$ decays. The precision of this measurement will be enhanced with increased data collection, allowing for the validation or rejection of the ${\rm SM}$ predictions, thus providing essential information for predicting other $C\!P$-violating modes such as $B_s^0\to \phi\pi^0$. The choice to measure $\phi_\phi$ and $\Delta A$ was based on considering theoretical uncertainties and practical measurement limitations. The results of fit procedures using published branching fractions and other study results for $\Delta A$ and $\phi_\phi$ have been examined, revealing that while $\phi_\phi$ is consistent with the ${\rm SM}$ prediction of $-21.1^\circ$, the measured value of $\Delta A$ of $0.063\pm0.014\ ({\rm stat})\pm0.013\ ({\rm syst})$ suggests a potential discrepancy from the ${\rm SM}$ prediction of $0.045\pm0.004$. The observed discrepancy has a significance of $2.3\,\sigma$, excluding random chance and experimental errors.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is heavily influenced by the movement of virus-carrying particles. Understanding this process is crucial in determining how environmental factors like airflow patterns, ventilation methods, and building pressure affect an occupant's exposure to pathogens. We develop a computational model that simulates respiratory secretions and aerosol dynamics within a typical bus. By analyzing virus-aerosol transport, we can identify key variables that impact aerosol behavior and identify critical moments when occupants may be at increased risk of exposure. Our study reveals that the majority of aerosol particles remain within the vehicle's interior, rather than being expelled outside, and that localized plumes can form around mouths emitting respiratory secretions. We further examine how building pressure differences impact these plumes and developed a method to quantify proximity and orientation between adjacent occupants that may facilitate aerosol transmission. We also evaluated the potential for three-seats in a row to serve as hotspots for respiratory droplet propagation, and discovered that vertical airflow can transport aerosols out of the vehicle. We developed a method to quantify the influence of these vertical air movements, and found that building pressure differences can significantly affect nearby occupants' exposure to airborne particles, even several rows away from the source of emission.

This study provides a comprehensive examination of the $\beta$-decay characteristics of proton-rich isotopes near the proton drip-line, particularly those within the Z = 19-24 range. We conducted $\beta$-decay calculations using the fp shell-model and evaluated the $ft$ values for key decay transitions. We also investigated the half-lives of even proton isotopes at the drip-line with neutron numbers N = 19-28. In an effort to select suitable candidates for isobar $\beta$-decay studies, we considered near-drip-line syzygies in the $(\beta^-, \beta^+) \ decay region, particularly focusing on odd-Z nuclei and investigating properties for $\beta$-decay transitions between odd-Z and odd-N nuclei and odd-Z and even-N nuclei. We also presented research findings for selected near-drip-line candidates that align with recently published near-drip-line nuclear data.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching.
Recent advancements include quantity-based double-sided auctions which enable multiple quantities to be traded per request.
Although these new methods offer more than the traditional double-sided auctions, their potential benefits remain largely unexplored.
We have developed a double-sided auction algorithm that supports quantity-based orders and efficiently executes multiple trades at once.
Simulations using real financial market data indicate that the new method:
help traders execute multiple trades without increasing transaction costs,
help market makers manage their inventory without requiring extra compensation,
have no significant impact on order book dynamics,
have no significant impact on traders' behavior.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be carried out within a specific non-expansive framework. Consequently, a series of examples are presented, primarily within finite non-metric metric spaces. These examples indicate that the proposed conjecture is likely incorrect in a general context, although the situation remains unknown for a particular type of metric space known as the tiling metric space.

Modern data-driven systems rely heavily on data for operation and decision-making. To keep up with advancements across industry, agriculture, industry 4.0, industry 5.0, industry 6.0, industry.research and other industry verticals as well as research. It's essential to develop predictive virtual models of these systems to ensure smooth operation and effective decision-making in real-time online environments. Modern advancements have led to complexities in three main areas: efficient communication, effective data management, and ensured data security. To address these challenges, this research aims to design a next-generation data-driven system that integrates online learning, data security, and efficient data handling within a unified virtual model. It's designed with confidence to ensure the digital health of system data and online transparency of system behavior to build system digital trustworthiness. To achieve this goal, this research proposes to address three core challenges at the heart of reliable decision-making in real-time online environments. Firstly, it develops a real-time online monitoring system that tracks the digital health of system data using an innovative approach of online metric aggregation with adaptive control parameters. Secondly, it ensures data security and transparency of system behavior using an original approach of online file authentication with secure keys update. Lastly, it ensures efficient system communication and storage at the system edge using an original approach of adaptive data age management with communication costs control. It is evaluated using two test cases of varying complexity with promising results demonstrating its effectiveness and high performance in real-time online environments with resource constrained systems

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the opening phase called "chess repertoire." Extensive databases of historical games have been compiled, allowing for an advanced understanding of opening strategies through an analysis of network properties among chess openings called relatedness network (RNN). Our research focuses on analyzing 1.7 million chess openings recorded up to 1995 moves, with a specific focus on position equivalence and game outcome equivalence, allowing for an exploration of network properties such as node degree distribution and clustering coefficients. The results of our study will help researchers better comprehend the evolution of chess openings and how it influences players' strategic development.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A general method exists for deriving constants of motion that extend beyond local bounds for ODE systems representing dissipative mechanical systems with dissipation. This method applies to both Lagrangian and Hamiltonian systems and can yield global constants of motion for certain systems, such as Rayleigh and Van der Pol oscillators. For these systems, we derive new energy-based estimates that guarantee the existence of solutions and give more precise bounds than standard ones. Furthermore, we develop a theory that guarantees the existence of solutions for Lagrangian systems where the dissipation coefficient is small but finite, and derive corresponding energy estimates.

Developing free online collections of 3D digital models has led to a significant challenge: helping users swiftly identify and choose the right model. Traditional methods of interacting with multiple models through visualizations like point clouds or meshes are not effective due to poor user experience. In this paper, we suggest an innovative interaction method that enables users to interact with multiple 3D models through air-drawing in a Virtual Reality setting. By capturing the relationships between simple 2D shapes, our framework predicts the corresponding model user-doodled, thus eliminating the need for visual overloading. Our framework prediction process involves learning the user's input and matching it with the target model through learning the user-data pairs, while also addressing potential drawing issues through error tolerance metric learning. Based on the experiment outcomes, our system proved to be efficient and practical for real-world applications.

HD 80606b, a planet resembling Jupiter, orbits its star with an extremely eccentric path, resulting in periods of both star-proximal and star-distant positions. Notably, its closest approach to the star lasts for a brief window within its orbital timeline, resembling a sudden burst of sunlight. Unlike its usual spectral observations conducted during the planet's long orbital phase, this study observes an unusual brief phase when the planet is in the sun-light bathed region. Utilizing two telescories during the planet's brief burst phase, our findings indicate that an analysis of its visible and infrared light signatures would have detected the planet's visible/spectral light emissions. These observations seem incompatible with a simple, two-layer model, instead suggesting a complex layering system, with a high-energy layer sitting atop a heat-carrying foundation.

In this investigation, we're looking at how self-similar solutions influence our understanding of gravitational collapse within a perfect fluid framework, where the state of the fluid is determined by its pressure and density, as well as its radial and temporal coordinates, when expressed in logarithmic form. Our focus lies on logarithmic perfect fluid self-similar solutions resulting from the collapse of a fluid ball under general relativistic conditions, applied to both Schwarzschild and anti-de Sitter spacetimes. Our analysis reveals that, aside from specific dust collapse cases, such self-similar solutions necessitate multiple spatial dimensions. Our consideration of additional fields facilitates only a minimal number of viable self-similar solutions, which possess temporal coordinates as an additional dimension. Our findings indicate that, due to these solution constraints, gravitational collapse through self-similar processes is not feasible in a single spatial dimension.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the alignment of this stress tensor with standard energy conditions. Specifically, it demonstrates that the corrections to extremality are directly related to the sign of the perturbation's energy. Furthermore, we have confirmed that these extremality corrections correspond to the standard area law at non-extremal points, and that all higher-order corrections converge. Notably, we have used this method to derive corrections to black hole entropy up to the second order, and verify that the Bekenstein-Schwartz mechanism for entropy reduction explains the inversion of extremality ratios.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize sample data to calculate the loss for each goal, enabling the training of policies that accurately produce goals when interacting with an environment. However, there are several challenges associated with this learning framework, including the difficulty of finding appropriate goal space transformations. A novel transformation is introduced in the paper, which spatially aggregates goal orientations while preserving the scale, thereby facilitating the discovery of valid goals through the policy. Additionally, the study focuses on maintaining a uniform distribution of goals, which is essential for efficient policy policy exploration. An efficient method is proposed to maintain this uniformity by reparameterizing the policy using a low-variance uniform distribution, even for tasks involving goal-oriented motor control. Experimental results are presented demonstrating the proposed method's effectiveness, which equals the performance of current state of the art uniform distribution methods while outperforming them in terms of efficiency and while also showing valid results in goal-oriented motor control.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a complex task, requiring agents to navigate through environments while interpreting visual goals. Traditional methods, such as incorporating navigation networks or using ground mapping, often struggle with scalability or fail to interpret complex goals. We introduce MemoNav, a novel memory-based approach that uses short-term visual memory to track an agent's movement and long-term memory, akin to human cognition, to link past experiences with current goals. By integrating memory with attention mechanisms, MemoNav achieves state-of-the-art results on the multi-room floor plan dataset, a challenging benchmark for image-based goal navigation.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially introduced 4G LTE using FDD, followed by DRS, subsampling, and significant power adjustments. However, these methods mostly addressed capacity issues while significantly impacting system spectrum and power efficiency. As various applications increasingly require more licensed spectrum than traditional cellular networks can provide, exploring spectral sharing between cellular and other services has emerged as a vital area of research. Unfortunately, existing cellular systems rely on strict guard bands, precluding effective spectral sharing. This study presents the first step towards a practical implementation of near-nominal band spectral sharing between WCDMA cells. We outline key technical challenges and propose initial solutions for filtering, sync, FDD, and power control, aiming to increase the capacity of existing WCDMA cells while maintaining backwards compatibility with existing networks. Power estimation is also used to determine power backing needs, with power control data from existing cells available to increase the capacity by 100% while halving power requirements.

We examine the statistical properties of hypergraphs formed from q-deformed
Gaussian processes, which generalize the well-known statistical distribution of
governor matrix factorizations. These findings have significant implications for
modeling complex interactions between multiple dynamic systems represented by
differentiated stochastic differential equations.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases how known examples of slow operator growth can be understood through the lens of Lie symmetry, while also demonstrating how two-mode coherent states serve as a straightforward and adaptable framework for studying complex systems with Lie symmetry.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}$C, has been a topic of discussion, with theories proposing it as an $\alpha$-condensate. However, the evidence for this is unclear. New research provides evidence against the Hoyle state being an $\alpha$-condensate by examining its decay into $^{8}$Be + $\alpha$ + $\alpha$ (8.6 MeV barrier), which was found to occur at a rate approximately one million times higher than expected if it were composed of condensed $\alpha$ particles. This higher decay ratio can be explained by a molecule-like structure, with the first electron shell excited.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture have achieved dynamic, three-dimensional simulations of breaking objects. Nevertheless, predicting crack paths in fast-moving, three-dimensional cracks through brittle materials remains a major unsolved issue. A significant gap exists in the physical understanding of how irregular crack patterns develop in 2D materials when the crack speed greatly exceeds typical wave speeds like sound or stress waves. Researchers studied the leading edge of fast-moving cracks using scaled speed and using light sources to visualize and record the track of rotating cracks, and found that the track speed varies along the perimeter and is highest where the crack rotates quickly. They discovered an area of lower speeds just behind the leading edge that influences the crack's rotation. Through theoretical analysis, they derived an equation for the track velocity that depends on the velocity of rotation and the energy release rate at the crack tip, demonstrating that and measuring the accuracy of this relationship. Numerical simulations of different materials with varying properties confirmed that and showed the relationship's applicability to predict rotating crack patterns in materials with differing speeds and properties.

In 1968, Berlekamp introduced the concept of feedback capacity for finite state channels, proposing a complex formula to calculate it. Over four decades later, the current approach to feedback capacity is still constrained by inefficient formulation and a lack of suitable optimization techniques. Our research presents a major breakthrough, specifically for the binary state binary symmetric channel, by reducing the intricate formula into a more manageable single expression. This allows for the application of optimization principles that were previously impossible. Our findings include the optimal feedback coding strategy, which involves symmetric independent actions, along with the minimum length of memory required to achieve this action. Additionally, our research pinpoints the optimal window size for likelihood approximation used in decoding. Our studies at low and high action levels reveal specific rates of capacity, namely 0.2203 and 0.5435, respectively, which exceed the lower bounds set by Berlekamp in 1968.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may serve as ideal candidates for topological superconductivity and host Majorana zero modes. Topological superconductors have the potential to lead to major breakthroughs in topological superconductivity-based, topological quantum, and Majorana-based research. We employed the tight-binding model and variational BCS formalism to investigate the influence of Rashba and Zeeman magnetic field and antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling on superconductivity in a two-dimensional spinless Tl-based electron gas substrate. Our results indicate that Rashba spin-orbit coupling alone is insufficient for topological superconductivity; however, combining Rashba with Zeeman magnetic field and antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling results in a promising environment for the emergence of topological superconductivity. Our study provides essential guidance for creating topological superconductors from Tl-based electron gas substrates.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduce a new dataset for Semantically Associated Tables (SemTab), along with two information verification tasks. These tasks involve determining whether information within a table is accurate or whether it can be found within the table itself. We then compare multiple large language models, including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, against a human baseline to evaluate their performance. Notably, we find that a simple rule-based method achieves comparable results to more complex language models for factual verification, while we observe the potential of specific models in answering questions with high precision and relevance.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations for distant groundwater flow.  I initially approached the subject by reading the book "Flow in Porous Media" by Childs and Collins, published in 1954, which provided the foundation for the summary presented here.  In order to understand the equations, I had to supplement the material from the book with additional information, particularly regarding matrix theory, which was not included in the original document.  I believe that a clear understanding of matrix theory, as well as other essential concepts, is crucial for mastering the derivation of the equations for distant groundwater flow.  I also found it helpful to refer to the book "A First Course in Numerical Analysis" by G. J. Abrahams, published in 2002, which provided the background information needed to understand the equations for the groundwater flow.

This work presents a revised model of gas-phase pollution oxidation that incorporates ozone and UV sunlight effects, in addition to surface interactions. The enhanced algorithm enables simultaneous calculation of ozone and UV radiation influence on pollutants, along with their byproducts and surface interactions. It also involves an ozone absorption coefficient, which determines the local ozone availability for reactions, and an average photon density, reflecting sunlight impact on chemical processes. The algorithm's efficiency is validated against experimental data for NOx oxidation in an ozone and UV light system, revealing excellent parameter alignment. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates consistency in results across various grid sizes and location variable methods, confirming its reliability for different simulation setups.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. No single simulation tool has emerged as the leader, forcing developers to run multiple simulations on various platforms. This presents a significant hurdle, given the rising complexity of the simulations and when combined with the need for multiple simulations, they can quickly become unaffordable. In response, an effort is being made to make these simulations more manageable by leveraging the multicore capabilities of modern systems, presenting an opportunity to share processing workload across cores. This work introduces an innovative approach to neural network simulation, showcasing how it enhances parallel execution on multi-core systems using VPXboards with Xilinx Zynq-7000 Processing Systems.

Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios often faces challenges due to uncertainties.
  Deploying such models in real-world settings often proves difficult due to inherent uncertainties.
  To address this, we introduce a novel model known as the Indecision Tree.
  This refined version of traditional Decision Trees incorporates mechanisms to handle uncertainties.
  It is based on the underlying principle that splits are chosen not only for maximum impurity reduction
  but also those with the highest confidence levels. We evaluate the efficacy of this model on various datasets,
  comparing its performance against established trees in terms of accuracy and the extent of uncertainties resolved.
  Notably, the results indicate that this model can provide interpretable paths even when classifications are uncertain,
  ultimately leading to improved accuracy rates.

DTW is a well-known but computationally intensive approach for time series matching.
 By simplifying DTW with early-exit strategies, EAP-DTWH (a prior proposal) achieves this by calculating the maximum additional distance between time series points ahead in the series.
 However, this method is flawed as this information may be unrepresentative due to the distorted path of the warping function.
  Our strategy takes a data-independent approach to simplify the DTW matrix, removing points that are close together along the diagonal using a variable step-size method.
  This simplification allows us to calculate the maximum additional distance more accurately, making it suitable for early-exit.
  Based on this, EAP-DTWH was developed with our accurate distance calculation instead of the approximate distance used in the prior proposal.
  It passed the rigorous T10 Resistance testing, significantly outperforming other early-exit DTW algorithms while maintaining the same performance as full DTW.

Current educational tools for testing students' understanding of code often focus on generating individual examples or faults, rather than using them as a means to assess multiple students simultaneously. Furthermore, the students themselves are not involved in the feedback loop, limiting their ability to improve their work based on the insights gained. To address these issues, a study is presented that explores testing and visualizing student performance metric metrics, including code coverage, based on university homework assignments. A visualization dashboard was developed to provide instructors with a view of student performance metrics, revealing patterns such as class-level coverage distributions and student familiarity with specific modules. Both instructors and students were shown the visualizations and provided positive responses, with students utilizing the insights to pinpoint areas for improvement, including module prioritization and bug selection for future testing exercises. The proposed tooling framework can be applied to various settings, from single students to large cohorts, serving both educational and evaluative purposes.

In domains requiring explainability and transparency, like healthcare, the features provided by AI machine learning models are often insufficient. Consequently, reliability and explainability become pivotal aspects. To address this, we've devised a methodology that enhances the reliability and clarity of AI models. Our method consists of two stages: the first involves developing a simpler, more interpretable model using feature selection to discover the main aspects of the data, while the second combines predictions from multiple high-accuracy "black-box" models to form an explainable and robust "composite model." The "composite model" is both more reliable and explainable than the individual "black-box" models, as evidenced by our experiments on three binary classification datasets. Statistical analysis confirms our composite model's performance is significantly superior.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it.

Dark matter particles interacting through "dark currents" may be accessible at particle colliders. A search for these particles at colliders is conducted with data collected at center-of-mass energies of 13 TeV by the CMS experiment at the LHC. Cases where the Z boson decays into either a pair of neutrinos or a pair of charged leptons (electrons or muons) are studied. An unusual excess of events is observed above statistical expectations, particularly when the number of extra charged particles produced alongside the Z boson is odd. This excess, with a local statistical significance of 2.8 sigma, is seen across a wide range of event momentum ranges. Considering system uncertainties, the observed results align less strongly with the predicted properties of dark matter particles, yielding a confidence level of 2.2 sigma. Consequently, the study's standard model background predictions are overabundant within this context.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, which is the main topic of the paper's methods to prove that product spaces of specific spaces with CSHP possess CSHP.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, confirming and understanding the remote epitaxial process remains a significant challenge. In this study, Heusler compounds with non-lattice-mismatched stoichiometry are employed to validate and investigate remote epitaxy of MnPtSn on exfoliated graphene grown on SiO2. Combining X-ray diffraction, low-energy electron diffraction, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that MnPtSn grows in a well-defined 30 degree rotated 2 x 2 orientation relationship with a well ordered honeycomb structure. The findings reveal that the remote epitaxy of MnPtSn on exfoliated graphene grown on SiO2 is influenced by the underlying substrate and SiO2.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, particularly when these patterns are difficult to capture using standard methods due to the presence of significant noise. A new approach, longmem, is introduced to infer these random patterns directly from data, without first having to simplify the data matrix. longmem relies on the relationship between complex statistical models and block structured submatrices within the data matrix. infers the patterns' characteristics by analyzing the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a data matrix, where "common patterns" are linked to the largest eigenvalues and those associated with the smallest eigenvalues, whereas those associated with intermediate eigenvalues represent noise. the method also provides eigenvalue and eigenvector estimation along with time series properties such as the spectral density, allowing it to work in high-dimensional settings with a large number of time series. the method has been validated through the same simulation datasets and an application to US monetary policy data.

Recent observations using the JWST have heavily utilized its powerful NIRCam and NIRSpec instruments to study NIR wavelength data, resulting in a profound upgrade in the quality of observations of NIR galaxies and a profound increase in the depth of observations using the Large Binocular Telescope (LBTE). A study analyzing data from six NIR galaxy surveys within three massive galaxy clusters at a redshift of approximately 2.0 discovered over a thousand new lensing events, specifically over-densities of galaxies likely affected by lensing, within the sampled area. This discovery led to a massive increase in the number of multiply lensed galaxies within this redshift range, providing new insights into the dynamics and mass distribution of massive galaxy clusters and a more accurate understanding of the distribution of galaxies within the redshift range. Data for a subset of these newly discovered lensed galaxies have been publicly released for further study to scientists.

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to financially support QoS enhancements in exchange for increased traffic from the ISPs. To find optimal outcomes, the paper develops closed-form solutions for quality and demand, as well as profitability, through a quality-based demand model, with and without regulatory limitations on sharing profits. By illustrating the advantages of such collaborations, the paper shows that agreements can generate higher levels of quality, demand, and profitability for all parties involved, with the optimal outcome potentially surfacing as a market equilibrium through decentralized negotiations between Content Providers and ISPs.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse procedure of passing from these abstract collections to their concrete matrix representations, a process analogous to specifically targeted functors that possess a reverse reconstruction functor in linear categories with concrete representations. We establish an analogous reconstruction theorem for *-algebras by showing that states can be reconstructed from their concrete predual Banach space representations. This is achievable as long as a state satisfies specific weak* continuity conditions on a collection of physical observables, which can be expressed as a weakly-* closed subspace of the algebra's multiplier C*-algebra. This reconstruction theorem also leads to a formula that calculates the reconstructed pre-dual Banach space from these continuity constraints.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory hold great promise in the context of upcoming cosmological observations, also having connections to supergravity.
